idiom_name: algebra interface over F + LanguageExt higher-kinded traits (K<F, A>, Monad, IO/Eff)
implementation_notes: C# has no higher-kinded types, but LanguageExt supplies the missing machinery: the `LanguageExt.Traits` namespace carries the higher-kinded trait types (a `K<F, A>`-style wrapper plus the `Monad`-family traits), and effect types such as `IO<A>`, `Eff<A>` and `Eff<RT, A>` give concrete constructors to instantiate F with. The algebra is therefore an ordinary interface generic in F (`interface Console<F> { K<F, Unit> PutLine(string s); }`), the program is a static generic method taking the dictionary, and each interpreter is a struct implementing the algebra for one F. What replaces the classic structure: the HKT trait machinery plus explicit dictionary parameters - C# resolves no instances implicitly, so the interpreter is passed at the call site (or injected). If the application has only one effect, `Eff<RT, A>` with an injectable runtime is the smaller realization: it drops the F parameter and injects the runtime instead.
pitfalls: Without an HKT wrapper the program can only be generic in a proper type, not in a type constructor: attempting `interface Console<F> { F PutLine(string s); }` fails to express `F<Unit>`, and every workaround costs an unchecked cast.

C# resolves no instances implicitly, so nothing stops two dictionaries for the same algebra from being in scope; the call site decides, and a wrong choice is a type error at best and a silent behaviour change at worst.

Struct interpreters are copied on every pass - keep them stateless or wrap state in a class; and nullable reference types plus `Unit` conversions make it easy to smuggle a `null` into the interpreted type.
